mainTopic: End of the משנה (local and spreading disasters, crying out on שבת, חוני המעגל, rain during a fast) and the start of the גמרא on when fasting begins and on מכת בצורת
overview: This amud finishes the third פרק of the משנה and begins the גמרא. When only one city suffers a local disaster, such as no rain, דבר or מפולת, that city fasts and cries out. Its neighbors do only one of these: the תנא קמא says they fast, and רבי עקיבא says they cry out. The משנה defines דבר, and it rules that spreading disasters like שדפון, ארבה, חיה רעה and חרב call for התרעה everywhere. It then lists dangers so urgent that we cry out even on שבת. Any public trouble calls for התרעה except too much rain, and the famous story of חוני המעגל and שמעון בן שטח's reaction illustrates this. The משנה also rules on when rain that falls during a fast day ends the fast, and it brings רבי טרפון's celebration in לוד as an example. The גמרא then resolves a contradiction about when fasting begins, with רב יהודה's reading and רב נחמן's limit on crops that dried out. Finally it explains the phrase מכת בצורת, and רב נחמן begins a statement that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The stricken city fasts and cries out; its neighbors only fast
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא rules that the afflicted city both fasts and does התרעה, while the surrounding towns fast but do not do התרעה.
steps.simpleTranslation: That city fasts and cries out, and all the towns around it fast but do not cry out.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה is continuing a case on the previous amud: a city where rain did not fall while other places got rain. It now tells us how that city and its neighbors respond.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The city actually suffering gets the full response, both a fast and התרעה. The neighbors are worried the trouble might reach them, so they show solidarity and concern by fasting. They do not do the more intense התרעה, because the disaster is not yet theirs.

keyTerms.meaning: fasts (observes a תענית)
cries out, by blowing שופר/חצוצרות or by crying out in prayer (התרעה)
its surrounding areas, the neighboring towns
an alarm-cry in response to a disaster

steps.confusionAlert: 'That city' is not introduced here. It refers back to the case in the משנה on the previous amud: a city with no rain while its neighbors had rain.

phrases.english: that city fasts and cries out,
phrases.notes: Refers to the city that alone did not receive rain (previous line of the משנה).

phrases.english: and all its surrounding areas fast but do not cry out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's earlier case of a city with no rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Afflicted city: fast + התרעה. Neighbors: fast only.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: the neighbors cry out but do not fast
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא disagrees about the neighboring towns. They do התרעה but do not fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: they cry out but do not fast.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא gives the opposite ruling for the surrounding towns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree the neighbors must do something, but not everything. The disagreement is which response fits them. The תנא קמא gives them the fast. רבי עקיבא gives them the התרעה instead.

keyTerms.meaning: the תנא who disagrees with the first opinion
but they do not fast

steps.confusionAlert: רבי עקיבא is talking only about the neighboring towns. He agrees the stricken city itself does both.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: מַתְרִיעוֹת וְלֹא מִתְעַנּוֹת.
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says: they cry out but do not fast.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes the תנא קמא's ruling for the neighboring towns.

steps.title: The same dispute applies to plague and collapsing buildings
steps.stepSummary: The משנה extends the same two-sided rule and the same dispute to a city hit by דבר or by מפולת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And likewise, a city that has a plague or collapsing buildings: that city fasts and cries out, and all its surrounding areas fast but do not cry out. רבי עקיבא says: they cry out but do not fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה uses the word וכן to say the exact same rules and dispute apply to two more local disasters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דבר and מפולת are like lack of rain: they strike one particular city. So the stricken city does both, and the neighbors do only one. The תנא קמא and רבי עקיבא keep the same positions as before.

keyTerms.meaning: and likewise, the same rule applies
plague, pestilence
collapse of buildings (e.g., weakened walls falling)

phrases.english: And likewise, a city that has in it
plague or collapsing buildings:
that city fasts and cries out,
and all its surrounding areas fast but do not cry out.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: מַתְרִיעוֹת וְלֹא מִתְעַנּוֹת.
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says: they cry out but do not fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן עִיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ דֶּבֶר אוֹ מַפּוֹלֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule and dispute of steps 1–2 to new disasters.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דבר and מפולת follow the same pattern as a city lacking rain, including the dispute with רבי עקיבא.
steps.whatToRemember: For a local disaster (no rain, דבר, מפולת), the stricken city fasts and cries out. Its neighbors do only one of the two. תנא קמא says they fast; רבי עקיבא says they cry out.

steps.title: What counts as a plague?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks for a definition of דבר.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is considered a plague?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה pauses to ask a definition question. This sets up the next step, which gives the exact measure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People die all the time, so we need a clear test for when deaths count as a plague that triggers fasting and התרעה. Without a definition, the rule in step 3 could not be applied.

keyTerms.meaning: which is, what is considered

phrases.english: What is considered a plague?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks to define a term used in step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The threshold at which deaths in a city are treated as דבר.

steps.title: Three deaths on three straight days in a city of 500 men
steps.stepSummary: A city that supplies 500 soldiers is in a plague if three people die on three consecutive days. Fewer deaths than that is not a plague.
steps.simpleTranslation: A city that sends out five hundred foot-soldiers, and three dead were taken out of it on three days one after another: this is a plague. Less than this is not a plague.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה answers its own question with a precise measure for דבר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The city's size is measured by how many able-bodied men it could send out as soldiers: 500. The pattern of deaths matters as well as the number: one death each day for three days in a row. If the deaths are fewer, or not spread out this way, it is not considered דבר.

keyTerms.meaning: foot-soldier, infantryman (an able-bodied man)
one after another, consecutively
less than this

steps.confusionAlert: 'Three dead on three days' means one death per day for three days in a row, not three deaths in a single day.

phrases.english: A city that sends out five hundred foot-soldiers,
and three dead were taken out of it
on three days, one after another:
this is a plague;
less than this, this is not a plague.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the definition question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: In a city of 500 men, three deaths on three consecutive days is דבר; fewer is not.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a practical threshold, so a community knows when to declare fasts for illness.

steps.title: Spreading disasters require crying out everywhere
steps.stepSummary: For שדפון, ירקון, ארבה, חסיל, חיה רעה and חרב, people do התרעה in every place, because these disasters travel.
steps.simpleTranslation: For these they cry out in every place: for blight, for mildew, for locusts, for caterpillars, for a dangerous beast, and for the sword. They cry out over it because it is a spreading disaster.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה lists a new category of disasters. These are not local like the earlier ones, so even faraway places cry out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 1–3 were about disasters that stay in one city, so the neighbors gave only a partial response. These disasters move from place to place, so everyone is truly in danger. That is why התרעה is done everywhere, not just in the stricken city.

keyTerms.meaning: in every place, even far from the disaster
blight, crops scorched by wind
mildew, crops turning sickly pale
a type of locust that comes in swarms
a dangerous wild beast
a 'walking' calamity, one that spreads

steps.whatToRemember: Local disasters: only the stricken city does the full response. Spreading disasters (מכה מהלכת): התרעה in every place.

phrases.english: For these they cry out in every place:
for blight, and for mildew,
and for locusts, and for caterpillars,
and for a dangerous beast, and for the sword,
they cry out over it,
phrases.notes: Read here, with Sefaria, as applying to the whole list; the גמרא later discusses how to read this clause.

phrases.english: because it is a spreading calamity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts spreading disasters with the local disasters of steps 1–3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For spreading calamities, התרעה is done in every place.

steps.title: A fast decreed everywhere for a tiny patch of blight in אשקלון
steps.stepSummary: The זקנים decreed a fast across the land after seeing שדפון in אשקלון, even though the patch was only the size of an oven's opening.
steps.simpleTranslation: An incident: elders went down from Jerusalem to their cities and decreed a fast because blight was seen in אשקלון, enough to fill the mouth of an oven.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה tells a story that shows the rule of step 6 in action: even a tiny amount of a spreading disaster, far away, caused a fast everywhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שדפון was on the list of מכה מהלכת. The story shows that even a very small amount is enough, because blight spreads. It also shows that distant cities responded, not just אשקלון.

keyTerms.meaning: an incident, a story brought to illustrate a law
the elders, the Sages
they decreed a fast
enough to fill the mouth of an oven, a small area

phrases.english: An incident: elders went down
from Jerusalem to their cities,
and decreed a fast because there was seen
blight the size of an oven's mouth in Ashkelon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the rule of step 6 with a real event.
steps.raayaObject: That שדפון, as a spreading disaster, requires a response everywhere, even in a small amount.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The fast decreed by the זקנים over blight in אשקלון.

steps.title: A fast decreed after wolves ate two children
steps.stepSummary: The זקנים also decreed a fast because wolves ate two children in עבר הירדן.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, they decreed a fast because wolves ate two children in Transjordan.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a second story, this time illustrating חיה רעה from the list in step 6.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wild animals attacking people is a sign of a dangerous beast in the area, which counts as a spreading threat. The fast was decreed beyond the place of the attack. The next step questions exactly what triggered it.

keyTerms.meaning: and furthermore, an additional case
wolves
Transjordan, east of the Jordan river

phrases.english: And furthermore, they decreed a fast
because wolves ate two children
in Transjordan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second illustrative story, about חיה רעה.
steps.raayaObject: That חיה רעה triggers a fast and התרעה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The fast decreed over wolves in עבר הירדן.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: the fast was because the wolves were only seen
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says the wolves did not eat the children. The fast was decreed just because wolves were seen in a settled area.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: not because they ate, but because they were seen.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי corrects the story in step 8. He says no one was eaten; the wolves were only seen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי יוסי is right, the rule is stricter: a dangerous beast merely appearing among people is enough to call a fast, with no need to wait for an attack. This matches the idea from the אשקלון story that a spreading danger is handled at its first sign.

keyTerms.meaning: the תנא who gives a different version of the story
that they were seen
not ..., but rather ...

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוסי is not saying no fast was decreed. He agrees there was a fast; he disagrees only about what caused it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא עַל שֶׁאָכְלוּ, אֶלָּא עַל שֶׁנִּרְאוּ.
phrases.english: not because they ate, but because they were seen.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: לֹא עַל שֶׁאָכְלוּ, אֶלָּא עַל שֶׁנִּרְאוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes the version of the wolf story given in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fast may be decreed when dangerous beasts are merely seen in a settled area.
steps.whatToRemember: Spreading disasters are handled at their first sign: a small patch of blight, or (according to רבי יוסי) wolves merely being seen, was enough to decree a fast.

steps.title: Dangers for which we cry out even on שבת
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists three emergencies that allow התרעה even on שבת: a city surrounded by enemies, a city threatened by a flooding river, and a ship in danger at sea.
steps.simpleTranslation: For these we cry out even on שבת: for a city surrounded by enemy nations or by a river, and for a ship being tossed about at sea.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a new list. These dangers are so urgent that we cry out even on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the list was about disasters that justify התרעה on weekdays. Here the משנה moves up a level: some dangers threaten lives right now, so we do not wait until after שבת. All three cases involve people who are trapped and in immediate danger.

keyTerms.meaning: We cry out or sound an alarm (with prayer or שופר)
On שבת
Non-Jews; here, enemy troops
A ship being tossed and endangered by a storm

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that saving lives in an emergency pushes aside the usual reluctance to cry out on שבת.

phrases.english: For these we cry out on Shabbat:

phrases.aramaic: עַל עִיר שֶׁהִקִּיפוּהָ נׇכְרִים אוֹ נָהָר,
phrases.english: for a city surrounded by gentile troops or by a river,
phrases.notes: A river that overflowed its banks and threatens to flood the city.

phrases.english: and for a ship tossed about at sea.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the list of weekday disasters and the stories about the זקנים, the משנה now states which dangers allow התרעה even on שבת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We cry out on שבת for a city surrounded by enemies or a flooding river, and for a ship in danger at sea.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: crying out on שבת is only to call for help
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says that on שבת the alarm is only to call people to help, not to cry out in prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: it is for help, and not for crying out in prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי adds a limit to the previous rule. On שבת the alarm is allowed only as a call for help.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion allows a full התרעה, prayer included, on שבת. רבי יוסי narrows this: the sound is permitted only to gather people who can physically help, such as soldiers or rescuers. Prayer-style crying out waits until after שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: Help; calling people to come and assist
Crying out in prayer to ה׳

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
For help, but not for crying out (in prayer).

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: לְעֶזְרָה וְלֹא לִצְעָקָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits what kind of התרעה is permitted on שבת in the cases of step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On שבת, crying out is permitted only to call for practical help, not for prayer.

steps.title: שמעון התימני adds plague, but the חכמים disagree
steps.stepSummary: שמעון התימני wants to add plague (דבר) to the שבת list, but the חכמים do not accept his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמעון התימני says: also for a plague. But the חכמים did not agree with him.
steps.whatsHappening: Another תנא tries to widen the שבת list to include a plague. The משנה tells us the חכמים rejected this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמעון התימני sees a plague as just as deadly as an enemy siege, so in his view it also allows crying out on שבת. The חכמים disagree, so a plague allows התרעה on weekdays but not on שבת. The phrase ולא הודו לו חכמים tells us his view is not the accepted ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Plague or deadly epidemic
The Sages did not agree with him (his view is rejected)

steps.confusionAlert: Plague is still a disaster for which we do התרעה on weekdays, as step 3 showed. The only dispute here is whether it also allows crying out on שבת.

phrases.english: Shimon the Timnite says:
Also for a plague,
but the Sages did not agree with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁמְעוֹן הַתִּימְנִי אוֹמֵר: אַף עַל הַדֶּבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a wider version of the שבת list from step 10, which the חכמים reject.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמעון התימני would cry out on שבת for a plague, but the חכמים rule that one does not.

steps.title: General rule: cry out for any public disaster except too much rain
steps.stepSummary: We cry out for every disaster that could strike the community, with one exception: too much rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: For any trouble that may (Heaven forbid) come upon the community, we cry out about it, except for too much rain.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a broad rule for all public troubles and names one exception, too much rain. It is also setting up the story of חוני המעגל that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording שלא תבוא ('that should not come') is a polite way of speaking about disasters that might come. Too much rain can cause damage, yet we do not cry out about it, because rain is basically a blessing. The story that follows illustrates this exception.

keyTerms.meaning: Trouble or disaster
The community or public
Too much rain

steps.confusionAlert: שלא תבוא does not mean a trouble that will not come. It is a respectful way of speaking, so we avoid saying outright that a disaster will come.

phrases.aramaic: עַל כׇּל צָרָה שֶׁלֹּא תָּבוֹא עַל הַצִּבּוּר
phrases.english: For any trouble that should not come upon the community
phrases.notes: A polite phrase meaning any trouble that might come.

phrases.english: we cry out over them,
except for too much rain.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל כׇּל צָרָה שֶׁלֹּא תָּבוֹא עַל הַצִּבּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the specific שבת list to a general rule for all public disasters, with one exception.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We cry out over every public disaster except too much rain.
steps.whyThisMatters: This exception is the reason the משנה tells the story of חוני המעגל.

steps.title: חוני is asked to pray for rain and his first prayer fails
steps.stepSummary: The people ask חוני המעגל to pray for rain. He confidently tells them to bring in their clay ovens so they will not dissolve, but no rain falls.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an incident where they said to חוני המעגל: Pray for rain to fall. He told them: Go and bring in the פסח ovens so they will not melt. He prayed, and no rain fell.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה begins a story to illustrate the exception of too much rain. In this first part, חוני prays confidently, but nothing happens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חוני is so sure his prayer will work that he warns the people to protect their clay ovens from heavy rain. When no rain falls, it sets up the bold step he takes next. The story will later show why one does not pray for rain to stop.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident or story
Honi the Circle-Drawer, a famous צדיק
Clay ovens used to roast the קרבן פסח
Melt or dissolve

phrases.english: There was an incident where they said to Honi the Circle-Drawer:
Pray that rain should fall.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: צְאוּ וְהַכְנִיסוּ תַּנּוּרֵי פְסָחִים
phrases.english: He said to them: Go out and bring in the Pesach ovens
so that they will not dissolve.
He prayed, and no rain fell.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the story that illustrates the exception of too much rain from step 13.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that one does not cry out over too much rain.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of חוני המעגל's prayers for rain.

steps.title: חוני draws a circle and swears not to move
steps.stepSummary: חוני draws a circle, stands inside it, and swears by ה׳'s name that he will not leave it until ה׳ has mercy on His children.
steps.simpleTranslation: What did he do? He drew a circle and stood inside it, and said before ה׳: Master of the World! Your children have turned to me, because I am like a member of Your household. I swear by Your great name that I will not move from here until You have mercy on Your children.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. After the failed prayer, חוני makes a bold move: he draws a circle and swears not to leave it until rain falls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חוני explains why he feels entitled to be so bold. The people relied on him because he is close to ה׳, 'like a member of the household'. His oath shows how far he is willing to go for the people, and it explains the name המעגל, 'the one who draws circles'.

keyTerms.meaning: He drew a circle
Like a member of the household; someone close and trusted
Swear or take an oath

phrases.english: What did he do?
He drew a circle and stood inside it,
and said before Him: Master of the Universe!
Your children have turned their faces to me,
because I am like a member of Your household.
I swear by Your great name
that I will not move from here
until You have mercy on Your children.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה עָשָׂה? עָג עוּגָה וְעָמַד בְּתוֹכָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story: after the failed prayer, חוני takes an oath inside a circle.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חוני swears not to move from his circle until ה׳ sends rain.

steps.title: חוני rejects drizzle and storms, and asks for blessed rain
steps.stepSummary: First only a few drops fall, and חוני says he asked for rain that fills cisterns. Then a violent storm comes, and he says he asked for gentle, blessed rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rain began to drip. He said: This is not what I asked for, but rain for pits, ditches, and caves. It began to fall violently. He said: This is not what I asked for, but rain of goodwill, blessing, and generosity.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. Twice the rain comes in the wrong form, and each time חוני corrects his request.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A drizzle is too little, since it cannot fill the water storage the people need for the year. A storm is too much and causes damage. חוני asks for the right balance, rain that is a blessing, and this sets up the next scene.

keyTerms.meaning: Dripping; falling in small drops
Cisterns, ditches, and caves used to store water
Violently, furiously
Goodwill, blessing, and generosity

phrases.english: Rain began to trickle down.
He said: This is not what I asked for,
but rain to fill cisterns, ditches, and caves.
It began to fall furiously.
He said: This is not what I asked for,
but rain of goodwill, blessing, and generosity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story: ה׳ answers the oath, and חוני adjusts what kind of rain he is asking for.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חוני asks not for drizzle or storms but for rain of blessing.

steps.title: Rain floods Jerusalem and חוני hints he will not pray for it to stop
steps.stepSummary: Normal rain falls nonstop until the people flee to הר הבית. They ask חוני to pray for it to stop, and he tells them to check whether the אבן הטועין has been washed away.
steps.simpleTranslation: The rain fell properly, until the Jews left Jerusalem and went up to הר הבית because of the rain. They came and said to him: Just as you prayed for it to fall, so pray for it to go away. He said to them: Go out and see whether the אבן הטועין has been washed away.
steps.whatsHappening: Here the story reaches the rule of step 13. The people ask חוני to pray for the rain to stop, and he answers with a hint that he will not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rain is now the right kind, but there is so much of it that people must leave their homes. חוני's reply means that as long as the huge אבן הטועין is still standing, things are not bad enough to pray against good rain. This illustrates that one does not cry out over too much rain.

keyTerms.meaning: In their proper way
The Temple Mount, which stands on higher ground
The Claimants' Stone, a large stone in Jerusalem where lost items were announced and claimed
Washed away, erased

steps.confusionAlert: חוני is not sending them to check for real. His answer is a polite way of saying the stone will never wash away, so he will not pray for the rain to stop.
steps.whyThisMatters: This scene is the reason the משנה tells the story. It shows the exception of too much rain in action.

phrases.english: They fell in their proper manner,

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיָּצְאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל מִירוּשָׁלַיִם לְהַר הַבַּיִת
phrases.english: until the Jews went out of Jerusalem to the Temple Mount
because of the rain.
They came and said to him:
Just as you prayed over them that they should fall,
so pray that they should go away.
He said to them: Go out and see
whether the Claimants' Stone has been washed away.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָרְדוּ כְּתִקְנָן, עַד שֶׁיָּצְאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל מִירוּשָׁלַיִם לְהַר הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The story reaches its point: a request to pray against too much rain, which חוני turns down.
steps.raayaObject: The rule from step 13 that one does not cry out over too much rain.
steps.raayaSupportSource: חוני's hint that he will not pray for the rain to stop while the אבן הטועין still stands.

steps.title: שמעון בן שטח's reaction to חוני
steps.stepSummary: שמעון בן שטח tells חוני that he deserves נידוי for his bold behavior toward ה׳. He cannot impose it, because ה׳ gives חוני what he wants, like a father with a beloved son who nags him.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמעון בן שטח sent a message to חוני: "If you were not חוני, I would declare you excommunicated. But what can I do to you? You nag ה׳, and He does what you want, like a son who nags his father and the father gives him what he wants. About you the verse says: 'Let your father and your mother be glad, and let her who bore you rejoice.'"
steps.whatsHappening: The story of חוני ends with the leader of the generation, שמעון בן שטח, judging what חוני did. He criticizes חוני and also praises him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Drawing a circle, swearing by ה׳'s name, and making demands of ה׳ looks disrespectful, so normally it would earn a נידוי. שמעון בן שטח holds back because ה׳ clearly answered חוני, which shows a special father-son closeness. The verse from משלי is used to say that חוני's parents should be proud of him.

keyTerms.meaning: The נשיא, the head of the סנהדרין, in חוני's time
Excommunication; a ban that separates a person from the community
Nags or pleads like a spoiled child, using closeness to get what he wants
"The Place"; a name for ה׳

steps.whatToRemember: חוני's prayer worked, but his way of praying was so bold that it nearly earned him נידוי. Only his special closeness to ה׳ protected him.

phrases.english: Shimon ben Shetach sent word to him:
Were you not Choni,
I would decree excommunication upon you.
But what can I do to you,
since you nag before God
and He does your will for you,
like a son who nags his father
and he does his will for him;
and about you the verse says:
"Let your father and your mother be glad,
and let her who bore you rejoice."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the חוני story by giving the authoritative reaction to his conduct.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: חוני's boldness deserved נידוי, but his unique closeness to ה׳ exempted him.

steps.title: Rain falling in the middle of a fast day
steps.stepSummary: If rain falls during a fast for rain, the תנא קמא says the fast ends only if the rain came before sunrise. רבי אליעזר says the fast ends if the rain came before midday.
steps.simpleTranslation: If people were fasting and rain fell for them before sunrise, they do not finish the fast. If it fell after sunrise, they finish it. רבי אליעזר says: before midday, they do not finish; after midday, they finish.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a new rule. When the fast's purpose, rain, is fulfilled during the day, do people keep fasting until night?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree that early rain cancels the fast and late rain does not. They disagree only about the cutoff time. The תנא קמא sets it at sunrise, and רבי אליעזר sets it later, at midday.

keyTerms.meaning: Sunrise
They must complete the fast until nightfall
Midday, halfway through the daylight hours
A תנא who argues with the first opinion

phrases.english: If they were fasting and rain fell for them,
before sunrise, they do not complete the fast;
after sunrise, they complete it.
Rabbi Eliezer says:
before midday, they do not complete it;
after midday, they complete it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the חוני story and opens a new halachic topic in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain before the cutoff ends the fast. The cutoff is sunrise according to the תנא קמא and midday according to רבי אליעזר.

steps.title: רבי טרפון ends the fast in לוד
steps.stepSummary: In לוד, rain fell before midday on a fast day. רבי טרפון told the people to eat, drink, and celebrate, and in the afternoon they said הלל הגדול.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once a fast was declared in לוד, and rain fell before midday. רבי טרפון told them: "Go out, eat, drink, and make it a festive day." They went out, ate, drank, and made it a festive day. Toward evening they came back and recited הלל הגדול.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings a real-life story that matches רבי אליעזר's view. The rain fell after sunrise but before midday, and the fast was ended.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the תנא קמא's sunrise cutoff, the people in לוד should have kept fasting. רבי טרפון ended the fast because the rain came before midday, which fits רבי אליעזר. The story also shows that answered prayer calls for celebration and thanks.

keyTerms.meaning: An incident; a story brought as a practical example
A city in ארץ ישראל
A תנא who ruled in this incident
Afternoon, toward evening
"The Great Hallel", תהלים קלו, which thanks ה׳ for His kindness, including providing food for all creatures (נוֹתֵן לֶחֶם לְכׇל בָּשָׂר)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the regular הלל said on holidays. הלל הגדול is a different chapter of praise, תהלים קלו.

phrases.english: An incident where they decreed a fast in Lod,
and rain fell for them before midday.
Rabbi Tarfon said to them:

phrases.aramaic: צְאוּ וְאִכְלוּ וּשְׁתוּ וַעֲשׂוּ יוֹם טוֹב,
phrases.english: Go out, eat, drink, and make it a festive day;

phrases.aramaic: וְיָצְאוּ וְאָכְלוּ וְשָׁתוּ וְעָשׂוּ יוֹם טוֹב,
phrases.english: and they went out, ate, drank, and made it a festive day,
and they came in the afternoon
and recited the Great Hallel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a practical incident that matches רבי אליעזר's midday cutoff.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אליעזר's view that rain before midday ends the fast
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי טרפון's ruling in לוד when rain fell before midday

steps.title: The גמרא quotes the משנה about the first rainfall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins by quoting an earlier line of the משנה: the order of fasts applies at the time of the first rainfall.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: "The order of these fasts that was stated applies to the first rainfall."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It quotes a line from the משנה so it can compare it to a ברייתא in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה earlier described a sequence of fasts that start when rain is late. This line says that sequence starts once the time of the first rainfall passes without rain. That timing is about to be challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that analyzes the משנה
The order, or sequence, of fasts
The first rainfall of the season, or its expected time

phrases.english: GEMARA:
phrases.notes: Marks the start of the גמרא section

phrases.english: The order of these fasts
that was stated is for the first rainfall.

steps.triggerLanguage: סֵדֶר תַּעֲנִיּוֹת הָאֵלּוּ הָאָמוּר בִּרְבִיעָה רִאשׁוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא by quoting an earlier line of the משנה, preparing for a contradiction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the משנה, the order of fasts begins at the first rainfall.

steps.title: A ברייתא says fasting starts only at the third rainfall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא contrasts the משנה with a ברייתא. The ברייתא says that at the first and second rainfalls we only pray for rain, and fasting begins only at the third.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they contrasted it with a ברייתא: "At the first and second rainfall, one asks for rain; at the third, one fasts!"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a contradiction. The משנה says fasting starts at the first rainfall, but a ברייתא says fasting waits until the third.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sources talk about the same situation, rain that has not come. They give different starting points for fasting, first rainfall versus third. The גמרא will now need to explain how both can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: "And they contrasted it"; the formula for raising a contradiction between two sources
To ask, meaning to pray for rain
To fast
The third rainfall

steps.confusionAlert: Here the word לשאול means praying and asking for rain. It is not a question about הלכה.

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
The first and second rainfall are for asking;
the third is for fasting!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה line quoted in step 21 with a conflicting ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's statement that the order of fasts begins at the first rainfall
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says the first and second rainfalls are only for prayer and fasting begins at the third, which directly conflicts with the משנה's timing.

steps.title: רב יהודה explains what the משנה really means
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה reads the משנה so that it no longer contradicts the ברייתא. The regular order of fasts applies only when the first, second, and third rainfall periods all pass with no rain. If rain fell in the first period and the crops then failed, we cry out immediately.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: This is what the משנה means. When does the order of fasts described here apply? When the first, second, and third rainfall periods have passed and no rain has fallen. But if rain fell in the first rainfall period, and people planted, and nothing sprouted, or it sprouted and then turned bad, we cry out about it right away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction from step 22. רב יהודה explains that the משנה and the ברייתא are talking about two different situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא describes the regular order, where fasting starts only after the third rainfall period passes with no rain. The משנה's mention of the first rainfall refers to a different case: rain did fall, but the crops then failed. In that case the damage is already visible, so we cry out immediately and do not wait.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means. The גמרא is rereading a source to explain it correctly.
A rainfall period. There are three expected periods in the rainy season.
They sprouted (the plants grew).
They changed, meaning the crops' appearance became worse.
They cry out or sound an alarm, a public emergency response.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the משנה and the ברייתא disagree. After רב יהודה's reading, the משנה's order of fasts, like the ברייתא, begins only after three rainfall periods with no rain. The words 'first rainfall' belong to a separate case: rain fell, but the crops failed afterward, and then we cry out immediately.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule: damage to crops that can be seen right now requires an immediate response, while a simple delay in the rain follows the slower order of fasts.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: this is what it is saying:
the order of fasts that is stated, when does it apply?
when the first rainfall period has passed
and the second and the third, and no rain fell.
But if rain fell in the first rainfall period
and they sowed but nothing sprouted,
or alternatively, it sprouted and then changed for the worse,
they cry out about it immediately.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא raised in step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the משנה and the ברייתא refer to different situations.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to require fasting already at the first rainfall, while the ברייתא delays fasting until the third.
steps.terutzMaskana: The regular order of fasts begins after three rainfall periods with no rain. If the first rain fell and the crops then failed, we cry out at once.

steps.title: רב נחמן limits the rule to crops that turned bad
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says we cry out only when the crops changed for the worse. If they dried out completely, we do not cry out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: This applies only when the crops changed for the worse. But if they dried out completely, we do not cry out.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן adds a limit to רב יהודה's rule about crying out right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Crops that look sickly can still be saved, so prayer can help them. Crops that have fully dried out are gone, and praying for them would be a pointless prayer. So the alarm applies only while there is still something to save.

keyTerms.meaning: Specifically, only in this case.
They dried out completely.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: specifically when they changed,
but if they dried out, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the case of crops changing, which רב יהודה mentioned in step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We cry out only for crops that changed for the worse, not for crops that dried out completely.

steps.title: Isn't רב נחמן's point obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב נחמן needed to say this, since the משנה already uses the word 'changed.'
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious! We learned the word 'changed' in the משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן's statement as unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source text says 'changed,' not 'dried out.' So it seems clear without רב נחמן that dried-out crops are not included. Why would he need to teach it?

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious. This challenges a statement for adding nothing new.
We learned (in a משנה).

phrases.english: It is obvious; we learned 'changed'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's statement from step 24 as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's statement that dried-out crops do not get an alarm.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wording of the source already says 'changed,' so excluding dried-out crops is obvious.

steps.title: The point covers dried crops that later grew stalks
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן's point is needed for crops that dried out and then produced stalks. You might think new stalks show the crops can recover. He teaches that we still do not cry out.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where they produced stalks. You might have said that producing stalks is something significant. So he teaches us that it is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רב נחמן is teaching something new about a harder case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If dried crops later grow stalks, it looks like a sign of life, so you might think prayer could still save them. רב נחמן teaches that these stalks do not count. The crops are still treated as dried out, so we do not cry out.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case. This shows a statement does teach something.
Where they produced stalks.
Stalk formation.
Lest you say. This introduces a mistaken thought the teaching comes to correct.
It teaches us.

phrases.english: No, it is needed where they produced stalks.
Lest you say that producing stalks is significant,
he teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 25 by finding a case where רב נחמן's point is not obvious.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Making the statement necessary (לא צריכא): it applies to a less obvious case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Dried crops that grew stalks might count as recovering, so we would cry out for them.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even dried crops that grew stalks are treated as dried out, and we do not cry out for them.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: We cry out only for crops that can still be saved. Fully dried crops do not count, even if stalks appear.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה's line about a break in the rain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: rain stopped for a period between one rainfall and the next. The full line says forty days.
steps.simpleTranslation: And likewise, if the rain stopped between one rainfall and another, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה. This is a setup for the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'and so on' points to the rest of the line in the משנה. It says that if forty days pass between rains, we cry out because it is מכת בצורת. The גמרא brings this line now so it can explain that phrase.

keyTerms.meaning: They stopped (the rains ceased).
And so on. The rest of the quoted line is left out.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן שֶׁפָּסְקוּ גְּשָׁמִים בֵּין גֶּשֶׁם לְגֶשֶׁם כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: And likewise, if rain stopped between one rainfall and another, etc.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן שֶׁפָּסְקוּ גְּשָׁמִים בֵּין גֶּשֶׁם לְגֶשֶׁם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new line of the משנה after finishing the discussion of crop damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A forty-day break between rainfalls is a reason to cry out.

steps.title: What does 'plague of drought' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the משנה means by the phrase מכת בצורת.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a 'plague of drought'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the meaning of a phrase in the משנה. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A forty-day gap is a delay in the rain, not yet a full drought. So the גמרא wants to know why the משנה calls it a plague of drought.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it? This asks for a definition.
A plague of drought.

phrases.english: What is 'a plague of drought'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a phrase in the line of the משנה quoted in step 27.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of מכת בצורת in the משנה.

steps.title: A plague that leads to drought
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, quoting רב, explains that the phrase means a plague that leads to drought.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: It is a plague that brings about a drought.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about the meaning of מכת בצורת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The forty-day gap is not yet a drought. It is a dangerous sign that will lead to drought if it continues. So we cry out now, before the full drought arrives.

keyTerms.meaning: That brings about, that leads to.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
a plague that leads to drought.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: מכת בצורת is a plague that leads to drought, not a drought that has already arrived.

steps.title: רב נחמן begins: from river to river
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן begins a statement about food being brought from one river area to another. The statement continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: From one river to another river...
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן starts a new statement that further explains the levels of drought. The sentence is not finished here and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is a place with no crops that must bring in food by river from another place. רב נחמן will tell us how that situation is classified. His ruling appears on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: From one river to another river, meaning food is brought in by river from another place.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:
from one river to another river...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion of drought by starting to describe a level of food shortage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The statement is incomplete here. The ruling on food that must be brought in from river to river continues on the next amud.
